title: Lazarus and the Rich Man
hook: Is the story of Lazarus and the rich man a tour of hell, or a parable about money?
tldr: It is a parable about stewardship and the love of money, not a map of the afterlife. Lazarus is Eleazar, God's Help, Abraham's faithful Gentile steward; the rich man in purple and linen stands for Judah's religious elite. His basanos is a touchstone test that purifies, not endless torture.
big_idea: A parable against loving money, not a literal description of hell.

points.title: It is a parable
points.text: Jesus spoke to crowds only in parables, it follows the Shrewd Manager parable on stewardship, and it uses classic Jewish parable imagery like Abraham's bosom.

points.title: Selective literalism
points.text: Hellfire readers take the fire literally but treat Abraham's bosom as heaven. Literally, Lazarus would sit on Abraham's chest, and heaven and hell would be a short walk apart.

points.title: Lazarus is Eleazar, God's Help
points.text: Hebrew names carry meaning. Eleazar recalls Abraham's Gentile steward from Damascus, disinherited when Isaac was born yet faithful, now receiving Abraham's inheritance.

points.title: The rich man is Judah
points.text: Purple means kingship, linen priesthood. A son of Abraham with five brothers, he stands for Israel's religious and wealthy leadership who ignored Moses, the Prophets and their Messiah.

points.title: Basanos: a touchstone
points.text: Basanos was a dark stone used to test gold's purity. The rich man's state is a testing that purifies, temporary and corrective, not sadistic neverending torment.

points.title: The great chasm
points.text: The chasm referred to the Jordan Rift Valley dividing Gentile lands from the Holy Land: a moral lesson on the finality of choices, not afterlife geography.

sections.summary: After the Shrewd Manager parable ends with you cannot serve God and wealth, Jesus tells of a rich man in purple and fine linen and a sore-covered beggar, Lazarus, at his gate, longing for table scraps while dogs lick his sores. Lazarus dies and angels carry him to Abraham's bosom (kolpon). The rich man, in Hades and basanos, asks for water, is told of a great chasm, begs a warning for his five brothers, and hears they have Moses and the Prophets.

sections.h: How we know it is a parable
sections.summary: First, Jesus spoke to the crowds only in parables (Matthew 13:34). Second, it uses terms and imagery typical of ancient Jewish parables. Abraham's bosom appears only once in the Bible but is a well-known Jewish metaphor (Apocalypse of Zephaniah 11:1-2, Kiddushin 72b, Genesis Rabba 67) for peace and blessing, not a literal place. The parable says nothing about faith: the religious rich man stands for the Pharisees, Lazarus for the poor vindicated as the Beatitudes promise.

sections.h: What If It's Not a Parable?
sections.summary: Augustinian-Calvinist readers must treat the story as history to keep literal hellfire, yet read selectively. John MacArthur calls Abraham's bosom kind of an Old Testament reference to heaven because Abraham was a true believer. False: the phrase is not in the Old Testament at all. He shifts the focus from the love of money (verse 14) to who is a true believer, though faith is never mentioned. Jesus had just told the Shrewd Manager parable about stewardship; he did not suddenly switch to narrating history.

Bosom means chest; literally, Lazarus would sit on Abraham's chest with no room to breathe. Literal reading also puts heaven and hell a short walk apart, able to talk, contrary to hell below and heaven above. The impassable chasm teaches the finality of ignoring God's commands, not afterlife geography. The great chasm referred to the Jordan Rift Valley, dividing Gentile lands from the Holy Land of promise, a symbol of salvation. Jesus had already said I speak in parables (Luke 8:10).

Hellfire advocates say a real name makes it history, but Hebrew names always carry meaning: Isaac means he will laugh, after Sarah's laughter; Samuel means heard by God, after Hannah's prayer. Lazarus is the Greek form of Eleazar, God's Help, signaling divine aid. Longing for crumbs from the table identified Gentiles (Matthew 15:22-28). Laid at his gate echoes the Proselyte of the Gate: a Gentile convert keeping Jewish ethics and some rituals without circumcision or baptism, seen as second class.

sections.h: Eleazar of Damascus, the faithful steward
sections.summary: Lazarus-Eleazar beside Abraham recalls Eleazar of Damascus, Abraham's chief steward (Genesis 15:2-3), a Gentile who was heir until Isaac was born yet faithfully carried out Abraham's wishes at the cost of his inheritance. The beggar with nothing of earthly value captures that disinheritance, continuing the stewardship theme. Rabbis often used a name to evoke tradition, making Lazarus-Eleazar the focus, not the fictional setting: some who are last will be first (Luke 13:30).

The unnamed rich man wears costly purple and linen: wealth and status. He stays unnamed to elevate Lazarus. He calls Abraham father and is called son (Luke 16:24-25): a legal heir to Abraham's blessings. Purple signals kingship and linen priesthood, the heritage of Israel, specifically Judah. It is Jesus' critique of Israel's religious and wealthy leaders, a sarcastic reply to we are Abraham's descendants (John 8:33, 8:39), echoing John the Baptist (Luke 3:8). Lazarus, the faithful steward, enters everlasting habitations (verse 9).

The fire symbolizing the rich man's punishment says nothing about how long it lasts. In Judaism and the Hebrew Scriptures fire carries deep symbolism of purification, a subject treated in a later chapter.

Basanos is translated place of torment (NIV), horrible place (CEV) and place of pain (GNT). HELPS Word-Studies defines it as a touchstone: a black, silicon-based Lydian stone for testing the purity of gold and silver, which left a peculiar mark when rubbed with pure gold. Only later did it mean examination by torture, and sickness was often called torture. It signifies not vengeful torture but purifying, cleansing testing: temporary and corrective, not sadistic and neverending.

Lazarus is Eleazar, Abraham's Gentile steward who ate the crumbs, stayed faithful though disinherited, and received the inheritance. The rich man is possibly Judah, Israel's religious aristocracy with five literal brothers, kingship and priesthood, yet an unfaithful steward who had the oracles of God but did not respond to its Messiah. Amid the Pharisees' love of money, the parable critiques materialism and calls for care of the poor, as Moses and the prophets demanded. The rich are nameless; the poor get the name God Helps.

The story does not build a hellfire doctrine. It overturns the popular idea that wealth signals God's favor on religious people and critiques those neglecting justice and mercy. Jesus uses familiar Jewish concepts to challenge Pharisaic practice, not to endorse their views. Read it within Luke's narrative, its Jewish context and Jesus' ministry, as ethical teaching and spiritual reflection, not a literal description of eternal torture. Parables illustrate; they are not doctrinal textbooks.

mythfact.myth: Using a real name proves Lazarus was a historical person.
mythfact.fact: Hebrew names carry meaning. Eleazar means God's Help and evokes Abraham's steward, a common rabbinic technique.

mythfact.myth: Abraham's bosom is an Old Testament name for heaven.
mythfact.fact: The phrase never appears in the Old Testament. It is a Jewish metaphor for peace and blessing.
Basanos was a touchstone for testing gold's purity: a purifying, temporary and corrective test.

mythfact.myth: The parable is about true believers going to heaven.
mythfact.fact: It never mentions faith. It critiques the love of money and neglect of the poor.

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew name Eleazar, behind Lazarus, mean?
quiz.why: Eleazar means God's Help, a meaningful name pointing to divine aid and to Abraham's faithful steward.
It was a black Lydian stone used to test the purity of precious metals, implying purifying testing.

quiz.q: What do the rich man's purple and linen symbolize?
quiz.why: Purple signals kingship and linen priesthood, pointing to Judah and Israel's religious elite.

reflect: If the rich man's failure was neglecting the beggar at his gate, who is lying at yours?
